lead: Displacement work, also called boundary work, moving-boundary work or p dV work, is the work a gas does when it pushes a boundary such as a piston. For a quasi-static process it equals ∫p dV, the area under the process line on a p–V diagram, so it depends on the path. Engines, compressors and pumps run on it. Other work modes follow the same pattern of a driving force times a displacement: shaft work, electrical work, spring work, stretching a wire, surface-tension work, and the flow work that pushes mass across a control surface. This chapter gives the formula for each and works the common paths with numbers.
prereq: You need: the sign convention, quasi-static processes and the ideal gas equation.

sections.h3: Displacement work is the area under the p–V line

blocks.text: Let gas at absolute pressure p push a piston of area A through a small distance dx. The force is pA, so the work done by the gas is δW = pA dx = p dV, where dV = A dx is the change of volume. Adding up the small steps of a quasi-static process from state 1 to state 2:
W₁₂ = ∫ p dV  (from V₁ to V₂)
blocks.where: W₁₂ is the work done by the system in kJ; p is absolute pressure in kPa; V is volume in m³ (1 kPa × 1 m³ = 1 kJ). The integral needs p as a function of V along the path, which exists only for a quasi-static process.

blocks.text: Expansion (V₂ > V₁) gives positive work, done by the gas; compression gives negative work, done on the gas. The area under the line from V₁ to V₂ is the work, so different paths between the same states give different work. Round a cycle, the net work is the enclosed area: positive for a clockwise loop on p–V, negative for an anticlockwise one.

For the polytropic path, p₂ = p₁(V₁/V₂)ⁿ. The exponent n covers the others as special cases: n = 0 is constant pressure, n = 1 is pV = C, and n → ∞ is constant volume. For a slow adiabatic process of an ideal gas, n equals the ratio of specific heats γ, about 1.4 for air; non-flow processes treat these paths with the first law.

In a free expansion, gas rushes from a tank into an evacuated space. The volume grows, but no surface is pushed against any resistance, so no work is done: W = 0 even though dV is not zero. ∫p dV does not apply because the process is not quasi-static; if a gas expands quickly against a known constant outside pressure pₑₓₜ, the work it does on the surroundings is pₑₓₜ (V₂ − V₁).

Each mode is a generalised force times the change of a generalised displacement. The table gives the work done on the system for the last four, which is how they usually appear; with this book's convention, work done on the system is negative.

head: Mode
Force and displacement
Work
rows: W = 2πNτ for N revolutions; power Ẇ = 2πnτ/60 for n rpm
W = V I t for a steady current I (A) over time t (s)
W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²), k in N/m
W = ∫σ dA; a soap film has two surfaces
W = pV to push volume V across a control surface

blocks.text: Paddle-wheel (stirring) work is shaft work done on a fluid; it can only enter the fluid, never come back out as shaft work. Magnetic work, a field times a change of magnetisation, appears in a few syllabi only by name. Flow work is the energy needed to push fluid into or out of a control volume; it joins internal energy to form enthalpy in the steady flow energy equation.

items: Draw the boundary and the path on a p–V sketch.
Write p as a function of V, or note which property is constant.
Integrate from V₁ to V₂, or use the table.
Attach the sign: expansion positive, compression negative.
Check units: kPa × m³ = kJ; use absolute pressure.

figure.caption: The worked example’s gas expanding from state 1 to 0.20 m³ along three quasi-static paths. Work is the area under each path, so the same start and the same final volume give 120 kJ, 55.45 kJ or 45.37 kJ.

spec.aria: A pressure–volume plot starting at 800 kPa and 0.05 cubic metres. A dashed horizontal line stays at 800 kPa; a curve pV = C falls to 200 kPa; a steeper curve pV to the power 1.3 = C falls to 131.95 kPa at 0.20 cubic metres, with the area under it shaded. Boxes give the three works: 120, 55.45 and 45.37 kJ.

examples.question: A gas at 800 kPa occupies 0.05 m³ in a cylinder. It expands quasi-statically to 0.20 m³. Find the work done by the gas if the path is (a) constant pressure, (b) pV = constant, (c) pV¹·³ = constant. Find the final pressure in (b) and (c) and comment.
steps: Check (c) by summing: splitting 0.05 to 0.20 m³ into many thin strips and adding p ΔV gives 45.37 kJ, the same value.

Comment: all three start at the same state and end at the same volume, but the work is 120, 55.45 and 45.37 kJ. The steeper the pressure falls, the smaller the area under the path (Figure 1.7.1). All are positive because the gas expands.
examples.answer: (a) 120 kJ; (b) 55.45 kJ with p₂ = 200 kPa; (c) 45.37 kJ with p₂ = 131.95 kPa.

examples.question: Gas in a cylinder pushes a piston against the atmosphere (100 kPa) and a linear spring. As the volume grows from 0.040 m³ to 0.080 m³, the gas pressure rises linearly from 150 kPa to 350 kPa. Find the work done by the gas, the work done against the atmosphere and the work stored in the spring (neglect the piston's weight and friction).
steps: The pressure is linear in V, so W = ½(p₁ + p₂)(V₂ − V₁) = ½ × (150 + 350) × (0.080 − 0.040) = 250 × 0.040 = 10.0 kJ, done by the gas.
Work against the atmosphere: pₐₜₘ ΔV = 100 × 0.040 = 4.0 kJ.
The rest goes into the spring: 10.0 − 4.0 = 6.0 kJ.
Check from the spring's side: the spring's share of the pressure is p − pₐₜₘ, rising linearly from 50 kPa to 250 kPa, so its work is ½ × (50 + 250) × 0.040 = 6.0 kJ. The two agree.
examples.answer: W = +10.0 kJ by the gas: 4.0 kJ against the atmosphere and 6.0 kJ stored in the spring.

traps: kPa × m³ gives kJ, not J: 800 kPa × 0.15 m³ = 120 kJ.
W = p(V₂ − V₁) holds only at constant pressure; on a pV = C path the pressure falls and the work is smaller (55.45 kJ, not 120 kJ).
Use absolute pressure in ∫p dV. Gauge pressure gives only the work beyond what the atmosphere absorbs.
Free expansion does no work even though the volume increases; ∫p dV does not apply to it.
In (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1), find p₂ from pVⁿ = C first; do not use the isothermal p₂.

quiz.q: Write the displacement work for a polytropic process pVⁿ = C.

quiz.a: The work needed to push a volume V of fluid across a control surface against pressure p: pV, or pv per kg.

quiz.q: Why is the work in a free expansion zero although the volume increases?
quiz.a: Work needs a resisting force moving through a distance. Expanding into a vacuum, the gas pushes against nothing, so no work crosses the boundary; the process is not quasi-static, so ∫p dV does not apply.

quiz.q: Why does a clockwise cycle on a p–V diagram give positive net work?
quiz.a: The expansion runs along the upper line and the compression along the lower one, so the positive area under expansion is larger than the negative area under compression; the difference, the enclosed area, is positive.

quiz.q: A gas is compressed at constant 150 kPa from 0.40 m³ to 0.25 m³. Find W.
quiz.a: W = 150 × (0.25 − 0.40) = −22.5 kJ: 22.5 kJ of work is done on the gas.

quiz.q: A paddle in a rigid tank is driven by a torque of 12 N·m at 300 rpm for 5 minutes. Find the work on the gas.
quiz.a: Revolutions N = 300 × 5 = 1500. W = 2πNτ = 2π × 1500 × 12 = 113 097 J = 113.1 kJ done on the gas, so W = −113.1 kJ in this book's convention.

quiz.q: A spring with k = 400 N/m is stretched from x = 0.10 m to 0.20 m. Find the work input.
From the same initial state, a gas expands to the same final volume once along pV = C and once along pV¹·³ = C. Which path gives more work, and why?
quiz.a: pV = C gives more (55.45 kJ against 45.37 kJ in the worked example). Along pV¹·³ = C the pressure falls faster, so the curve lies lower and the area under it is smaller.

beyond: Indicator diagrams, the measured p–V loops of an engine cylinder, give the indicated work per cycle as their enclosed area; modern engines record them with fast pressure sensors and crank-angle encoders. Generalised work, a force times the change of its paired displacement, leads into the thermodynamics of elastic solids, dielectrics and magnetic materials, used in magnetocaloric cooling.
